name: monoio (io_uring thread-per-core runtime)
baseline: Tokio 1.14 multi-threaded runtime with one worker per core (current_thread at 1 core), serving the same TCP ping-pong server
verdict_reason: For a network server with many connections spread evenly over cores, monoio's peak QPS was 2.0x Tokio's at 4 cores and 3.0x at 16 cores; Tokio's QPS barely grew beyond 8 cores in this test (774526 at 8, 908179 at 16). At 1 core the gap was 1.13x, with few connections Tokio had lower latency, and the comparison is against Tokio 1.14 from 2021.
tier_reason: Public benchmark code (monoio-benchmark), raw results, server CPU, NIC, kernel and nightly toolchain all stated; first-party.
claimed_speedup: Best QPS, 100-byte ping-pong, monoio vs Tokio: 1 core 232888 vs 205726, 4 cores 868525 vs 430921, 16 cores 2764152 vs 908179 (1.13x, 2.0x and 3.0x, derived from page data). Text: 'about twice that of Tokio' under 4 cores and 'close to 3 times' under 16 cores.
workload: TCP ping-pong: client machines open a fixed number of connections per core, send 1 KB or 100-byte messages, and the server echoes them; best QPS across connection counts, servers on 1 to 20 cores, client and server on separate physical machines.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz server, Intel X710 10GbE NIC
platforms: Linux (io_uring on 5.6+, epoll otherwise) and macOS (kqueue)
one_liner: Thread-per-core io_uring runtime from ByteDance; 2-3x Tokio's peak QPS on a 4-16 core echo server in its 2021 benchmark.
how_it_is_fast: Each core runs its own single-threaded executor and io_uring instance, and connections never move between threads, so there is no work-stealing synchronization and tasks need not be Send. I/O is submitted in batches through the ring instead of one readiness syscall per operation, and buffers are passed by ownership to the kernel.
use_it_when: Proxies, gateways and load balancers whose connections can be sharded evenly across cores
Servers on 4 or more cores that saturate Tokio's multi-threaded scheduler
skip_it_when: Unbalanced workloads: the README warns idle cores cannot help busy ones
Few connections or single-core deployments, where Tokio matched or beat it on latency
Code that depends on the Tokio ecosystem (hyper, tonic, tower) without adapters; monoio's ownership-based I/O traits differ
caveats: Tokio 1.14 (2021) and nightly-2021-11-26; both runtimes have changed since and no newer comparison was found.
First-party benchmark on the authors' production network; one workload (echo).
Monoio's last crates.io release is 0.2.4 (2024-08) even though the repository is active.
tradeoffs: Tasks are pinned to their thread, so one hot connection can saturate a core while others idle.
io_uring needs Linux 5.6+ and a raised memlock limit.
Separate I/O traits limit reuse of Tokio-based libraries.

evidence.quote: Under single core, Monoio's performance is slightly better than Tokio; under 4 cores, the peak performance is about twice that of Tokio; under 16 cores, it is close to 3 times.
In the case of a single core and very few connections, Monoio's latency will be higher than Tokio, resulting in lower throughput than Tokio.
If the workload is very unbalanced, it may cause performance degradation than Tokio since CPU cores may not be fully utilized.
